tip: Adverbs compare with -τερα: νωρίς (norís = early) becomes νωρίτερα (norítera = earlier) – no extra word for 'more' needed.
One verb covers both: χάνω (cháno) is 'lose' and 'miss' – μη χάσεις τη βόλτα (mi chásis ti vólta) = don't miss the walk.
Time is passed, not had: περάσαμε τέλεια (perásame télia) is literally 'we passed perfectly' – Greek's way of saying we had a great time.
εδώ και τρεις μήνες (edó ke tris mínes) = literally 'here and three months'. With plain present ψάχνω (psáchno) it means 'I've been looking for three months now'.
The 'me' goes before the verb: θα με πάρουν (tha me pároun) = literally 'they'll me take'. In statements, short object pronouns slot in front of the verb.
Stacking negatives is correct Greek: δεν με πήραν ποτέ (den me píran poté) = literally 'they didn't take me never' – that's the standard way to say 'never'.
'Call back' is 'call again': ξανα- (xana = again) glues onto the verb – θα ξαναπάρω (tha xanapáro) = I'll call again. Never παίρνω πίσω (pérno píso = take back).
You 'make an application': έκανα αίτηση (ékana aítisi) = I applied. The lookalike εφαρμόζω (efarmózo) means implement, not apply for a job.
Where English uses 'to', Greek links verbs with να: ελπίζω να βρω (elpízo na vro) = I hope to find – there's no plain infinitive to fall back on.
Dropping by is 'passing': να περάσω για μια κουβέντα (na peráso ya mia kouvénda) = literally 'to pass by for a chat' – περνάω (pernáo) covers casual visits.
This και isn't 'and': δεν έχω και πολλή εμπειρία (den ého ke polí embiría) = I don't have all THAT much – και adds a shrug to negatives.
One word carries the wish: μακάρι να μου τηλεφωνήσουν (makári na mou tilefonísoun) = 'if only they'd phone me' – μακάρι να + verb is 'I wish/hope'.
'Careful not to' is πρόσεξε να μην (prósexe na min) – literally 'watch that not': να μην έχει ορθογραφικά λάθη (na min échi orthografiká láthi) = that it has no spelling mistakes.
Languages wear the article: στα αγγλικά (sta angliká) = literally 'in the English'. Plain σε αγγλικά (se angliká) sounds off – the article is not optional.
No 'for' needed: περιμένω απάντηση (periméno apántisi) = literally 'I await answer' – περιμένω takes its object directly.
'What should I...?' is just τι να + verb: τι να βάλω; (ti na válo) = what should I wear? No word for 'should' appears.
Greek says 'show' where English says 'look': να μη δείχνεις αγχωμένος (na mi díchnis anchoménos) = literally 'not to show stressed'.
κρατάω (kratáo = hold) also means 'last': η συνέντευξη κράτησε (i sinéndefxi krátise) = the interview 'held', i.e. lasted, about half an hour.
Hiring is 'taking': δεν με πήραν (den me píran) = literally 'they didn't take me' – everyday Greek for not getting the job.
The passive lives in the ending: πληρώνονται (plirónonde) = 'they are paid' – no word for 'are'. One verb form does the whole job.
You ask FROM someone: ζήτησα από το αφεντικό (zítisa apó to afendikó) = literally 'I asked from the boss' – ζητάω (zitáo) marks the person asked with από.
The idiom carries a dummy 'them': τα πάω καλά με (ta páo kalá me) = literally 'I go them well with' = get along with – the τα refers to nothing.
Being late is a verb: αργώ (argó). Πάντα αργεί (pánda aryí) = literally 'he always lates' – no 'is' involved.
One verb English lacks: προλαβαίνω (prolavéno) = 'have time to, make it in time'. Δεν προλαβαίνω να τελειώσω (na telióso) = I can't fit finishing in.
Receipts get 'cut': κόβω απόδειξη (kóvo apódixi) = literally 'I cut a receipt' – the standard phrase for issuing one.
λόγω (lógo) = 'because of', and the next word shifts to its of-form: λόγω της κρίσης (lógo tis krísis) = 'by reason of the crisis'.
μένω (méno = stay) covers ending up in a state: έμεινα άνεργος (émina ánergos) = literally 'I stayed unemployed' = I was left jobless.
A dummy-'them' idiom: τα βγάζω πέρα (ta vgázo péra) = literally 'I get them across' = I make ends meet.
Off-the-books work is 'black': μαύρη εργασία (mávri ergasía) = literally 'black work' – the everyday term for undeclared jobs.
Fear takes its own linker: φοβάμαι μήπως (fováme mípos) = literally 'I fear lest' – μήπως adds the 'what if' English handles with 'might'.
Contributions are 'stuck on' like stamps: κολλάνε ένσημα (koláne énsima) = literally 'they stick stamps' – from the days of paper pension booklets.
Retiring is 'coming out': θα βγω στη σύνταξη (tha vgo sti síndaxi) = literally 'I'll come out into the pension'.
'In order to' is για να + verb: για να ανοίξω (ya na aníxo) = 'so that I open' – Greek has no plain infinitive, so να does the work.
Withdrawing is 'lifting': σήκωσα πενήντα ευρώ (síkosa penínda evró) = literally 'I lifted fifty euros' – the everyday way to say it.
Cards 'pass': δεν πέρασε η κάρτα (den pérase i kárta) = literally 'the card didn't pass' – the standard phrase for a declined card.
Money 'enters': μπήκε ο μισθός (bíke o misthós) = literally 'entered the salary' – verb first, and the pay does the moving.
After a warning, μη attaches straight to the verb: πρόσεξε μη δώσεις (prósexe mi dósis) = 'watch out you don't give' – no να needed.
One verb, two directions: δανείζω (danízo) = lend, δανείζομαι (danízome) = borrow – the card's δάνεισε (dánise) = he lent.
μακάρι να + past tense = an unreal wish: μακάρι να μπορούσα (makári na boroúsa) = 'I wish I could' – the past form signals it isn't happening.
μην + present forbids the habit: μην ξοδεύεις (min xodévis) = 'don't be spending (ever)'. A one-off ban uses the other form: μην ξοδέψεις (min xodépsis).
The school level takes the of-form: πρώτη δημοτικού (próti dimotikoú) = literally 'first (grade) of primary' – no word for 'grade' needed.
περνάω (pernáo = pass) also means getting accepted: πέρασα στο πανεπιστήμιο (pérasa sto panepistímio) = I got into university.
In the past, μπορώ shifts meaning: μπόρεσα (bóresa) = 'I managed to', not just 'I was able'. Δεν μπόρεσα να τελειώσω (na telióso) = I didn't manage to finish.
Teachers split by school level: δασκάλα (daskála) = primary teacher; καθηγήτρια (kathiyítria) from secondary school up. Different jobs, different words.
δεν... καθόλου (den... kathólou) = 'not... at all' – a stacked negative that's correct Greek: δεν μου αρέσει καθόλου (den mou arési kathólou).
